title: Pressure-driven laminar flow between two parallel plates

summary.headline: Verification passed. The simulation reproduces the exact solution: on the finest mesh (128 cells across the gap) the velocity profile differs by \(0.0061\,\%\) of \(u_{\max}\).

findings: The error falls about \(4\times\) each time the cells are halved: observed order \(p = 2.00\), the scheme is designed for \(p = 2\). The solver behaves as intended.
Wall friction balances the driving force to \(6.8 \times 10^{-13}\) on every mesh: momentum is conserved and every run converged.
For 1 % accuracy, \(N_y = 16\) cells across the gap are enough (0.33 s).
limitations: Periodic ends force fully developed flow. A real channel needs an entrance length before this profile forms; that region is not modelled.

problem.description: Water flows between two very large parallel plates, driven by a constant pressure gradient. Find the steady flow and compare the simulation with the exact solution.
setup: Two stationary plates a distance \(H\) apart, so large that the flow depends only on the position \(y\) across the gap.
A constant pressure gradient \(dp/dx\) along the plates drives the flow.
Both plates are no-slip (the water sticks to them).

rows.name: Laminar flow (smooth layers, no turbulence)
rows.check: \(Re_H = \dfrac{\bar u\, H}{\nu} = 497\). In the units used by stability theory, \(Re = \dfrac{u_{\max}\,(H/2)}{\nu} = 373\), below the linear-stability limit 5772 (Orszag 1971) and below the observed transition ≈ 1000 (Carlson et al. 1982, approximate).

rows.name: Incompressible (density constant)
rows.check: \(Ma = \dfrac{u_{\max}}{c} = 5 \times 10^{-5} \ll 0.3\), with speed of sound in water c ≈ 1482 m/s (approximate).

rows.name: Steady and fully developed
rows.check: \(\partial u/\partial t = 0,\ \partial u/\partial x = 0\). Enforced by the steady solver and the periodic ends. Holds in a real channel only far from its inlet (after the entrance length).

rows.name: Two-dimensional
rows.check: The plates are very wide, so nothing changes across the width (\(z\)).

rows.name: Newtonian fluid, constant properties
rows.check: Water is Newtonian (stress proportional to strain rate); constant temperature, so \(\rho\) and \(\nu\) are constant.

rows.name: Gravity does not affect the flow
rows.check: Gravity acts across the gap; it only adds a hydrostatic pressure variation in \(y\) and does not change \(u\).

rows.name: No slip at both plates
rows.check: A viscous fluid in contact with a solid wall moves with the wall: \(u = 0\).

theory.intro: This problem has an exact solution. It is derived and solved symbolically by SymPy, not in the agent's reasoning, and checked automatically against the equation and both boundary conditions.

steps.label: Governing equation: x-momentum for steady, fully developed flow
steps.note: The pressure force pushing the fluid forward is balanced by viscous friction between layers.

steps.label: Boundary conditions: no slip at both plates
steps.note: Fluid touching a stationary wall does not move.

steps.label: Solution: integrate twice, apply both conditions
steps.note: A parabola: zero at the walls, fastest in the middle.

derived.label: Maximum velocity
derived.why: The fastest fluid, on the centreline (y = H/2). It is what a velocity probe in the middle of the gap would read.

params.meaning: driving pressure gradient, \(G = -\,dp/dx\) (pressure falls along the flow)

derived.label: Flow rate per unit width
derived.why: Volume of fluid passing per second, per metre of plate width. This is what a pump must deliver, and in design it is usually the requirement.

params.meaning: driving pressure gradient, \(G = -\,dp/dx\) (pressure falls along the flow)

derived.label: Mean (bulk) velocity
derived.why: Average velocity over the gap, \(\bar u = q/H\). It enters the Reynolds number and pressure-drop correlations. For this parabola \(\bar u = \tfrac{2}{3}u_{\max}\).

params.meaning: driving pressure gradient, \(G = -\,dp/dx\) (pressure falls along the flow)

derived.label: Wall shear stress
derived.why: Friction stress the fluid exerts on each plate; times the plate area it gives the drag force. It must balance the pressure force: \(2\tau_w = G H\) (two walls, per unit area).

params.meaning: driving pressure gradient, \(G = -\,dp/dx\) (pressure falls along the flow)

self_checks.name: Solution satisfies the momentum equation \(\mu\, u'' = -G\)
Solution display form \(\frac{G}{2\mu}\, y\,(H - y)\) equals the derived solution

decisions.why: Re is about 500 (laminar, see Assumptions); water is Newtonian; \(Ma \approx 5\times10^{-5}\).
decisions.affects: Defines the equations solved. A turbulence model here would add viscosity that does not exist and give a flatter, wrong profile.
decisions.alternatives: A transient solver would reach the same steady state, only slower.

decisions.why: The question asks for the steady state only; a steady solver gets there directly.
decisions.affects: None on the converged answer; it decides how the answer is reached.
decisions.alternatives: pimpleFoam (transient) run until steady; icoFoam has no body-force support.

decisions.choice: Short channel slice with periodic (cyclic) ends; length \(L_x = 0.1\,H\), one cell thick in \(z\)
decisions.why: Periodic ends make the slice behave like an infinitely long channel, which is the fully developed flow the problem describes. One cell in \(z\) with empty front/back makes it 2D.
decisions.affects: Imposes \(\partial u/\partial x = 0\) exactly. Entrance effects of a real channel are excluded by construction.
decisions.alternatives: A long channel with inlet and outlet: needs the entrance length (\(\sim 0.05\,Re\,H\)) and gives a developing flow near the inlet.

decisions.choice: No slip on both plates: \(\mathbf{u} = 0\); pressure zero-gradient at the walls
decisions.why: Stationary solid walls. Zero-gradient pressure is the standard partner of a fixed-velocity wall.
decisions.affects: Sets the shape of the profile (zero at both walls).
decisions.alternatives: None physically sensible for this problem.

decisions.choice: Initial state: fluid at rest, \(\mathbf{u} = 0,\ p = 0\)
decisions.why: A steady, linear problem has one solution regardless of the starting guess.
decisions.alternatives: Start from the analytical profile (would hide solver problems, so not used).

decisions.choice: Pressure gradient applied as a uniform body force \(a = -\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{dp}{dx}\)
decisions.why: Periodic ends cannot carry a net pressure drop. A uniform force per unit mass has the identical effect on the fluid.
decisions.affects: Drives the flow. Its magnitude sets every velocity linearly.
decisions.alternatives: A fixed pressure jump across the periodic boundary, or fixing the mean velocity (meanVelocityForce) instead of the gradient.

decisions.choice: Uniform meshes with \(N_y = 8, 16, 32, 64, 128\) cells across the gap; 1 cell along \(x\)
decisions.why: Refinement ratio 2 between meshes lets the observed order of accuracy and the mesh error be measured. Nothing varies along \(x\), so one cell suffices.
decisions.affects: Discretisation error; measured in the Comparison section.
decisions.alternatives: Cells clustered toward the walls (grading): more accurate near the walls for the same cell count, but a uniform mesh keeps the order-of-accuracy test clean.

decisions.choice: Second-order central schemes: Gauss linear for gradients, Laplacian and interpolation; corrected surface-normal gradients
decisions.why: Second order is the standard for accuracy; the mesh is orthogonal so no limiting or correction is needed. Convection is zero here, so the convection scheme (div(phi,U)) has no effect.
decisions.alternatives: First-order upwind for convection would add numerical diffusion in problems where convection matters.

decisions.choice: SIMPLE with NO under-relaxation (factors 1); plain SIMPLE, not SIMPLEC
decisions.why: The problem is linear (no convection), so one undamped iteration gives the answer. Relaxation 0.9 acted as a pseudo time step and needed thousands of iterations at 128 cells; SIMPLEC without relaxation divides by zero for pure diffusion (see Insights).
decisions.affects: Only how fast the answer is reached. Nonlinear problems DO need relaxation.
decisions.alternatives: Standard relaxation (U 0.7, p 0.3) converges slowly here.

decisions.choice: GAMG (multigrid) for \(p\) and \(\mathbf{u}\), solved to \(10^{-12}\) every iteration
decisions.why: Multigrid removes smooth, domain-wide errors quickly; a tight tolerance makes the iteration error negligible against the mesh error.
decisions.alternatives: PCG/DIC for p and smoothSolver for U: correct but slower on fine meshes.

decisions.choice: 5 SIMPLE iterations; results written at the end with 12 significant digits
decisions.why: Converges in 1 iteration; the rest confirm it stays put. More is worse: undamped round-off noise in \(p\) slowly grows. 12 digits avoid round-off in the error analysis (the default 6 digits broke an earlier analysis).
decisions.alternatives: A residual-based stop (residualControl): unusable here, see Insights.

decisions.choice: Wall shear stress on both plates; flow rate as the flux through the periodic boundary
decisions.why: These are requested outputs (c, d) and the momentum-balance convergence check needs the wall shear stress.
decisions.affects: How the reported quantities are measured.
decisions.alternatives: Integrating the velocity profile for q (adds its own quadrature error).

model.model: A short slice, length \(L_x = 0.1\,H\), with periodic ends: fluid leaving on the right re-enters on the left, so the slice behaves like an infinitely long channel.
2D: one cell thick in \(z\); nothing varies across the width.

An equivalent push on every fluid parcel, \(a = -\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{dp}{dx} = 0.006011\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\). Periodic ends cannot carry a pressure drop, so the gradient is applied as this body force; the effect on the fluid is identical.

notes: A residual measures how far the current solution is from satisfying the discretised equations. It drops to round-off (\(\sim 10^{-15}\)) after the first iteration, because the problem is linear.

Pressure is not plotted: it is zero everywhere in this problem, so its normalised residual is only round-off noise. Convergence is judged physically: the flow rate must stop changing (\(< 1 \times 10^{-10}\)) and the wall friction must balance the driving force (\(< 1 \times 10^{-8}\)).
Log checks: no crash, no NaN, no growing residuals or Courant number (automatic, cfdlib.monitor).

comparison.kind: Verification: the simulation is compared with the exact solution of the same equations.

definitions.name: Velocity-profile error
definitions.meaning: Typical (root-mean-square) difference over all cells, as a fraction of the peak velocity.

definitions.name: Flow-rate error
definitions.meaning: Relative error of the flow rate computed by OpenFOAM.

definitions.name: Observed order
definitions.meaning: \(\varepsilon \propto h^p\). \(p = 2\) means halving the cells cuts the error by 4.

definitions.name: Momentum balance
definitions.meaning: Must be zero on any mesh: friction on both walls balances the driving force.

findings: Where the error comes from. On every mesh the simulated profile is the exact parabola shifted up by a constant, \(\Delta u = \dfrac{G h^2}{8\mu}\) (cell-to-cell variation of the shift \(\le 1.3 \times 10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m/s}\), round-off). Inside the channel the method is exact for a parabola; the error enters at the walls, where the slope \(du/dy\) is estimated over the half cell between the wall and the first cell centre. Averaging the two middle cells cancels the shift, so the centreline velocity is exact on every mesh.

insights.problem: All runs stopped at the 5000-iteration limit, "not converged"; wall shear stress 0.4 % off on the finest mesh although it must be exact.
insights.diagnosis: Two causes. (1) The stopping rule used normalised residuals of \(v\) and \(p\), which are zero in this flow, so their normalised residuals are pure round-off noise and never fall. (2) Under-relaxation (U 0.9) acts like a pseudo time step: for diffusion-dominated problems each iteration removes only \(\sim 1/N^2\) of the smooth error, about 0.3 % per iteration at 128 cells.
insights.fix: Judge convergence physically (flow rate stops changing, wall friction balances the driving force). Linear problem: remove relaxation; it converges in 1 iteration.
insights.lesson: Normalised residuals are meaningless for fields that are ~0. Under-relaxation cost grows like \(N^2\) on diffusion-dominated problems.
insights.guideline: Always define a physical convergence check (a conserved quantity or balance). For linear problems use relaxation 1.

insights.problem: Removing relaxation crashed the solver with a floating-point exception on the first iteration.
insights.diagnosis: SIMPLEC (consistent yes) divides by \(A_P - \sum A_{nb}\), which is exactly zero for pure diffusion without relaxation.
insights.fix: Plain SIMPLE (consistent no) with relaxation factors 1.
insights.lesson: SIMPLEC needs either relaxation or a convection/time term.
insights.guideline: Do not combine SIMPLEC with relaxation factor 1.

insights.problem: With 20 undamped iterations the 128-cell run drifted after converging (flow rate changing by \(10^{-9}\)).
insights.diagnosis: Round-off noise in the (zero) pressure field grows a little each undamped iteration and feeds back into \(\mathbf{u}\).
insights.fix: Stop after 5 iterations; the answer is exact after the first.
insights.lesson: More iterations is not always safer when nothing damps round-off.
insights.guideline: For linear problems run a handful of iterations and confirm with the physical check.

insights.problem: An earlier analysis matched cells by their \(x\)-coordinate and got a wrong result on the finest mesh.
insights.diagnosis: OpenFOAM writes coordinates with 6 significant digits by default, so exact-coordinate matching is fragile.
insights.fix: Locate cells by grid index; write results with writePrecision 12.
insights.lesson: Never match cells by exact floating-point coordinates.
insights.guideline: Set writePrecision 12 and sample by index or with OpenFOAM sampling functions.

insights.problem: Shell commands passed from PowerShell to WSL lost quotes and parentheses.
insights.diagnosis: PowerShell re-parses the command line before WSL receives it.
insights.fix: Put every Linux command in a script file and run it with wsl ... -- bash script.sh.
insights.lesson: Never pass complex inline bash through PowerShell.
insights.guideline: Already in the skill: run Linux work from script files or the Python pipeline.
